title: Cross products as dual linear functionals: a duality-driven view in 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra (Chapter 11)
summary: This video presents a rigorous, principle-based route to understanding the 3D cross product by viewing it through the lens of linear transformations and duality. It begins with the familiar determinant-based construction of the cross product, where the second and third columns are the vectors v and w and the first column holds the symbolic basis vectors i-hat, j-hat, k-hat. By treating the resulting determinant as the coordinates of a resulting vector, it connects the familiar geometric facts—the cross product’s magnitude equals the parallelogram area spanned by v and w, and its direction is perpendicular to both with orientation given by the right-hand rule—to a deeper, dual-interpretive framework. The video then introduces duality for transformations from three dimensions to the reals, showing that a linear map to the number line can be represented as a dot product with a special vector p. By applying this idea to the determinant-based functional det[(x, y, z), v, w], the speaker derives p as the dual vector, tying the computational determinant trick to a geometric vector perpendicular to v and w with length equal to the parallelogram area. This dual viewpoint explains why the same computation produces the cross product and clarifies the projection-interpretation of the dot product with p, ultimately linking the algebraic and geometric pictures and foreshadowing the change of basis theme to come in the next video.

title: Determinant: Visualizing Area and Volume Scaling with Orientation (2D and 3D)
summary: This video builds an intuition for the determinant as the single scaling factor that a linear transformation applies to area in the plane (and to volume in space). Through concrete 2x2 and 3x3 examples, it shows how basis vectors are transformed, how an area changes for a unit square and a unit cube, and how orientation can flip when the determinant is negative. It also introduces the idea that the determinant is zero exactly when space collapses to a lower dimension, and it provides the 2x2 formula ad − bc with geometric intuition, before hinting at the multiplicative property det(AB) = det(A)det(B).

title: Dot products and duality: projection, matrices, and the transformation view
summary: In this 3Blue1Brown segment from Essence of Linear Algebra, the dot product is revisited not as a stand-alone computation but as a gateway to projections, linear transformations, and duality. The talk starts from the standard coordinate-wise definition and geometric projection interpretation, covers how dot products reflect whether vectors point in the same direction, are perpendicular, or oppose each other, and discusses the symmetry of the operation. It then builds a bridge to the matrix view by treating a 2D-to-1D transformation as a 1-by-2 matrix, illustrated with the Ihat, Jhat basis and a concrete example. A key move is embedding a number line diagonally in 2D space to show how a unit-vector projection corresponds to a 1-by-2 matrix acting on vectors, which leads to the core idea of duality: certain 1D-linear transformations correspond to specific vectors in the plane, and vice versa. The video culminates in a conceptual synthesis—dot products as a way to translate vectors into the world of transformations—before alluding to the cross product in the next video.

title: Change of Basis in Linear Algebra: Translating Vectors Between Coordinate Systems (Jennifer’s Basis)
summary: 3Blue1Brown’s chapter on Change of Basis explains how vectors and coordinates depend on the chosen basis. The video introduces standard basis vectors i-hat and j-hat, then presents Jennifer’s alternate basis b1 = (2,1) and b2 = (-1,1). It shows how a vector described in our coordinates (3,2) can be expressed in Jennifer’s coordinates as (5/3, 1/3) by forming the change-of-basis matrix from Jennifer’s basis and applying it to the vector. The inverse matrix translates in the opposite direction, enabling us to convert (3,2) to Jennifer’s language with coordinates (5/3, 1/3). The talk then connects these ideas to matrix-vector multiplication, viewing a matrix whose columns are Jennifer’s basis vectors as a transformation that maps our standard basis to Jennifer’s. It demonstrates how to rotate space (90-degree CCW) and how to compute the corresponding transformation in Jennifer’s language via A^{-1} M A, illustrating the idea of “empathy” between coordinate systems. The section concludes by tying these constructions to the general utility of changing basis and hints at eigenvectors and eigenvalues in a subsequent video.

title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: invariant directions and diagonalization
summary: 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra Chapter 14 visually introduces eigenvectors and eigenvalues as the invariant directions of a linear transformation. The video works through a concrete 2D example where the transformation stretches along specific lines (the x-axis and a diagonal line), then formalizes the eigenvector equation Av = λv, leading to the standard determinant-based eigenvalue computation det(A − λI) = 0. It shows how to extract eigenvectors by solving (A − λI)v = 0, gives concrete eigenvectors for the example (e.g., along (1,0) and (−1,1)), and discusses special cases such as rotations (which may have no real eigenvectors) and shear (limited eigenvectors). The concept of an eigenbasis is introduced, explaining how if a matrix has enough eigenvectors, changing to that basis diagonalizes the transformation, making computations such as high powers of A straightforward. The video also connects these ideas to change of basis and emphasizes when diagonalization is beneficial (and when it isn’t).

title: Polynomials as Vectors: Representing the Derivative as a Linear Operator
summary: In this episode from the Essence of Linear Algebra, the author broadens the notion of a vector beyond arrows or lists of numbers to include function spaces, and then uses polynomials as a concrete, infinite-dimensional example. Functions can be added and scaled just like vectors, and linear transformations (operators) preserve these two operations. A basis for polynomials is chosen using powers of x, rendering polynomials as coordinate vectors with infinite length (only finitely many nonzero terms). The derivative operator is then shown to be linear, and with respect to the polynomial basis it is represented by an infinite, mostly-zero matrix that shifts coefficients down the diagonal. A practical demonstration on a specific polynomial shows how the derivative corresponds to a matrix-vector product in this basis. The video culminates by framing linear algebra as a general theory that applies to many vector-like objects (arrows, numbers, functions, etc.) via a shared axiomatic structure of vector spaces and linear transformations.

title: Matrix multiplication as composition: interpreting linear transformations via basis vectors (Essence of Linear Algebra, Chapter 4)
summary: 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra, Chapter 4, presents matrix multiplication as the composition of linear transformations. The video recalls that a linear transformation is determined by the images of the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat, so the matrix columns encode these transformed bases. It then shows how composing two transformations (e.g., rotation followed by a shear) yields a single matrix—the product—that captures the overall effect. The derivation is illustrated both geometrically and numerically: you can obtain the composition matrix by tracking where each basis vector ends up through the sequence, or by applying the left matrix to each column of the right matrix. The right-to-left reading of products follows from function notation. The chapter also covers the order-sensitivity of composition, demonstrates a concrete 2×2 example, generalizes to symbolic matrices, discusses associativity from a transformation viewpoint, and ends by encouraging conceptual understanding over memorization while foreshadowing higher-dimensional extensions in the next video.

title: A quick trick for computing eigenvalues (2×2) from trace and determinant
summary: This 3Blue1Brown micro-lesson presents a fast method for finding eigenvalues of 2×2 matrices by using two already-available invariants: the trace (sum of eigenvalues) and the determinant (product of eigenvalues). The video shows that if you let the eigenvalues be λ1 and λ2, their mean m equals half the trace and their product p equals the determinant; then λ1 and λ2 are m ± sqrt(m^2 − p). After deriving and illustrating the method, the host works through concrete examples, including a quick matrix (3,1;4,1) and a second example (2,7;1,8), and then connects the idea to Pauli spin matrices in quantum mechanics. The video concludes with a comparison to the traditional characteristic-polynomial approach and discusses when this mean-and-product trick provides a speed advantage, especially for linear combinations of Pauli matrices. The segment also references a jingle by A Capella Science to mnemonic-ify the formula and ties the result back to broader quadratic-root ideas.

title: Cross products explained: 2D area intuition, 3D vector result, and a determinant-based construction
summary: This two-part module opener surveys the standard 2D cross product intuition as the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors, emphasizing how orientation (order of V and W) determines the sign and how a determinant computes that area via the matrix with V and W as columns. The video then shifts to the true 3D cross product, describing it as a vector whose length equals the parallelogram area and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane, determined by the right-hand rule. A mnemonic determinant procedure in 3D is introduced: form a matrix with I, J, K in the first column and the coordinates of V and W in the other columns, then take its determinant to obtain the cross product vector. The host notes deeper geometric ideas (duality) in a follow-up video and clarifies the distinction between the 2D signed-area intuition and the full 3D cross product.

summary: This video introduces the vector as a foundational concept in linear algebra, exploring three related perspectives (physics, computer science, and mathematics) and emphasizing the origin-centered geometric view. The core operations—vector addition (via the tip-to-tail method) and scalar multiplication (scaling)—are defined and illustrated, including how coordinates transform under these operations. The video also discusses the intuition behind these operations, why they are defined the way they are, and how the two representations (space-and-geometry versus numerical lists) interrelate. title: 2D Linear Transformations and their Matrix Representation (i-hat and j-hat)
summary: This video introduces linear transformations in two dimensions and shows how every such transformation can be encoded by a 2x2 matrix. It emphasizes visual intuition by treating input vectors as points on a grid and watching how the entire space is mapped while preserving straight lines and fixing the origin. The key idea is that the transformation is completely determined by where the two basis vectors i-hat and j-hat land; those two image vectors form the columns of the describing matrix, and all other vectors are obtained by linear combinations of these images. Concrete examples include a 90-degree rotation and a shear, with a clear formula for how a general vector (x, y) is mapped to x times the image of i-hat plus y times the image of j-hat. The video culminates in taking away the perspective that matrices are transformations of space, a viewpoint that clarifies later topics like matrix multiplication, determinants, and eigenvalues.

title: Inverse matrices, column space, and null space (Chapter 7) – Essence of Linear Algebra
summary: This video builds intuition for inverse matrices, the column space, rank, and the null space through the geometric lens of linear transformations. It frames linear systems as Ax = V, where A is a matrix of coefficients, X the unknown vector, and V the right-hand side. The discussion covers when A is invertible (nonzero determinant) and how the inverse A^{-1} undoes A to solve Ax = V, emphasizing that in the nonzero-determinant case there is a unique solution obtained by applying the inverse to V. The video also introduces the concepts of the column space (the set of all possible outputs of the transformation), rank (the dimension of that output space), and the null space (the set of vectors that map to zero), and it highlights how these ideas explain existence and form of solutions in a geometric way. Throughout, the focus is on intuition rather than computational methods, noting that practical calculation is typically left to software and that Gaussian elimination/row-echelon methods lie outside the scope of this particular presentation. The content also touches on the use of linear algebra in applications like computer graphics and robotics, and it signals that a future short footnote will cover non-square matrices.
